terms.register: vōx cōmica et poētica: Plaut., Hor.
evidence: Plaut. Men. 620–621: num ancillae aut servī tibi respōnsant?
terms.comment: The frequentative of respondeō; Lewis & Short glosses Plautus’s line “answer you back”. Horace uses it of standing up to one’s desires. Lewis & Short marks rē-; the house writes re- short before sp.

evidence: Cic. Q. fr. 2.8.1: ut mē et appellēs et interpellēs et obloquāre

terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase, of classical words: īnsolenter is “arrogantly, insolently”.

phrases.latin: Nōlī mihi respōnsāre; fac quod jubeō.
phrases.english: Don’t answer back; do as you’re told.

phrases.latin: Numquis servōrum dēlīquit? num ancillae aut servī tibi respōnsant? ēloquere. impūne nōn erit.
phrases.english: Has one of the slaves done wrong? Do the maids or the menservants answer you back? Tell me. They won’t get away with it.

phrases.latin: Etiamne, impudēns, muttīre verbum ūnum audēs aut mēcum loquī?
phrases.english: What, you cheeky thing, do you still dare say one word, or talk to me?

sources: Lewis & Short: responso · Lewis & Short: obloquor · Lewis & Short: insolenter
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 390.
